title: Permissions and environment variables
description: Master Linux permissions, ownership, and environment variable troubleshooting.

data.text: Linux permissions and environment variables control who can access files and how processes behave. In production, misconfigured permissions are a frequent cause of deployment failures, and missing environment variables can cause applications to crash on startup. Both are quick to diagnose once you know where to look.

Every file and directory in Linux has an owner and a group. Permissions are divided into three categories: read (r), write (w), and execute (x). These permissions apply separately to the owner, the group, and everyone else. You can view permissions with ls -l.

data.code:
ls -l /var/www/app/
# -rw-r--r-- 1 deploy deploy 1234 Jan 1 12:00 app.js
# owner=read+write, group=read, other=read

items: Read (r): view the contents of a file or list a directory
Write (w): modify a file or create/delete files in a directory
Execute (x): run a file as a program or enter a directory
Numeric mode: 755 means owner=rwx, group=rx, other=rx

data.text: A typical production issue is that the application runs as the deploy user but cannot read a config file owned by root. Another is that a script does not have execute permission and cannot start. Directories need execute permission for users to enter them, even if they have read permission.

data.code:
chmod 755 /opt/app/start.sh   # make script executable
chown deploy:deploy /opt/app/  # fix ownership
stat -c '%U %G %a' /opt/app/    # show owner, group, and permissions

data.title: Beware of 777
data.text: Giving everyone full access with chmod 777 might fix an error quickly, but it is a serious security risk in production. Always prefer the least privilege that solves the problem.

Environment variables are key-value pairs passed to a process when it starts. They are commonly used for configuration: database URLs, API keys, feature flags, and runtime settings. If a variable is missing or misspelled, the application may crash or behave unexpectedly.

You can inspect the environment of a running process through /proc/[pid]/environ. This file contains all environment variables separated by null bytes. The env and printenv commands let you view or set variables in your current shell.

data.code:
cat /proc/1234/environ | tr '\0' '\n' | grep DATABASE
printenv | grep APP_

items: Can the application read its config file? Check ownership and permissions with ls -l
Is the script executable? Check with ls -l and add execute permission if needed
Are required environment variables set? Check /proc/[pid]/environ
Does the service user have access to the working directory? Check directory permissions

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: Permissions control who can read, write, and execute files
Directories need execute permission for traversal
Environment variables are loaded at process startup
Check /proc/[pid]/environ to inspect a running process environment
Avoid chmod 777 in production; use least privilege
